5.3. Model Dirichlet Problems and Harmonic Rigidity🔗

The ball and half-space constructions provide the weak maximum principle and Poisson uniqueness used by the checked mean-value argument. Mean values then lead to derivative estimates, stronger maximum principles, Harnack comparison, and Liouville rigidity.

5.3.1. Green Kernels and Poisson Representation🔗

Green's functions convert Dirichlet problems into integral representations. Given boundary data g on \partial\Omega and interior forcing f, the solution of -\Delta u=f in \Omega, u=g on \partial\Omega, is formally represented by

u(x)=\int_\Omega G(x,y)f(y)\,dy -\int_{\partial\Omega}\frac{\partial G}{\partial\nu_y}(x,y)g(y)\,dS(y).

Evans (2010, pp. 33–41) derives this representation and symmetry for bounded C^1 domains, then computes explicit kernels on the half-space and ball. Gilbarg and Trudinger (2001) (Chapter 2) give a more classical treatment emphasizing the potential-theoretic perspective. We follow the explicit model-domain route first: construct the kernels, prove their off-pole properties, and solve the Dirichlet problem on the ball. The representation and symmetry theorems on general bounded C^1 domains come after the ball.

5.3.1.1. The Ball Kernel and Dirichlet Problem🔗

Kelvin inversion places an image pole outside the ball, so subtracting the image fundamental solution produces a kernel that is harmonic away from the physical pole and vanishes on the sphere. The negative outward normal derivative -\partial_{\nu_y}G_B(x,y) is the Poisson kernel, and the associated Poisson extension is regular, harmonic, recovers its boundary values, and is the unique such solution.

To make the construction concrete, consider the three-dimensional unit ball. The fundamental solution is \Phi_3(x)=1/(4\pi|x|). For an interior pole x\in B(0,1) with x\ne0, the Kelvin image is x^*=x/|x|^2, which lies outside the ball since |x^*|=1/|x|>1. The Green's function is then

G_B(x,y)=\frac{1}{4\pi|y-x|}-\frac{1}{4\pi|x|\,|y-x^*|}.

On the boundary sphere |y|=1, the identity |y-x|=|x|\,|y-x^*| makes the two terms cancel, confirming G_B(x,y)=0. The outward normal derivative of G_B is negative; its negative gives the Poisson kernel

K_1(x,y)=\frac{1-|x|^2}{4\pi|x-y|^3}\qquad(|y|=1).

This explicit formula shows that the Poisson kernel is positive, singular as x\to y\in\partial B, and has mass one over the sphere. For the ball of radius r, scaling replaces |x|^2 by |x|^2/r^2 and introduces the appropriate dimensional normalization (Evans, 2010, pp. 40–41; Gilbarg and Trudinger (2001), Theorem 2.6).

In positive dimension, write x^*=x/\lVert x\rVert^2 when x\ne0. The unit-ball Green kernel is the total function

G_B(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{(1-\max\{x_0,y_0\})(1+\min\{x_0,y_0\})}{2},&n=1,\\[4pt] \Phi_n(y-x)-\Phi_n\!\left(\lVert x\rVert(y-x^*)\right),&n\geq2,\ x\ne0, \end{cases}

with the continuous x=0 branch written explicitly in Lean. The first variable is the physical pole and the second is the field point; in the one-dimensional branch, x_0 and y_0 denote their sole coordinates. For n\geq2 the kernel is the Kelvin construction of Evans §2.2.4; for n=1 it is the Dirichlet kernel of -d^2/dx^2 on (-1,1).

    Green's function for the unit ball.

    For n = 1, this is the Dirichlet Green kernel for -d²/dx² on (-1, 1). For n ≥ 2, it is Evans's formula (41) in §2.2.4(c). Boundary vanishing and classical harmonicity away from the pole are proved below for n ≥ 2; the one-dimensional properties and the distributional identity -Δ_y G(x, ·) = δ_x are not.

The defining property of a Green kernel is that it vanishes when the field point reaches the boundary. For the Kelvin construction this is the inversion identity \lVert y-x\rVert=\lVert x\rVert\,\lVert y-x^*\rVert on the unit sphere, which gives the two fundamental-solution terms arguments of equal norm.

Proof for Theorem 5.30
uses 0

Write x^*=x/\lVert x\rVert^2 for the Kelvin image of a nonzero pole. For \lVert y\rVert=1, the inversion identity gives

\lVert y-x\rVert =\lVert x\rVert\,\lVert y-x^*\rVert =\bigl\|\lVert x\rVert(y-x^*)\bigr\|.

Thus the physical and image arguments of the fundamental solution have the same norm, so the two terms in the Green kernel cancel. The proof treats dimension two and dimensions at least three separately because the fundamental solution is logarithmic in the former and a negative power in the latter. If x=0, both formulas reduce directly using \lVert y\rVert=1.

Boundary vanishing concerns the sphere; harmonicity concerns the interior. For a nonzero interior pole the image x^* lies outside the closed ball, so both fundamental-solution terms are harmonic in y throughout B(0,1)\setminus\{x\}. Harmonicity off the pole together with vanishing on the sphere makes G_B a Green kernel.

Proof for Theorem 5.31
uses 1

Expand the Kelvin-inversion formula. Each fundamental-solution term is harmonic away from its pole, and the geometric hypotheses keep both relevant poles outside the point where the field-variable Laplacian is evaluated.

The Poisson kernel is the negative outward normal derivative -\partial_{\nu_y}G_B(x,y) on the sphere, in which the two fundamental-solution terms combine into a single closed expression. We take that closed form, scaled to a ball of radius r, as the definition of the kernel, following Evans's computation of -\partial_{\nu_y}G_B; the theorems about the Poisson extension work from the formula directly.

For a positive radius r, the ball Poisson kernel is

K_r(x,y)=\frac{r^2-\lVert x\rVert^2} {n\alpha(n)r\lVert x-y\rVert^n}.

Its boundary-value interpretation uses x\in B(0,r) and y\in\partial B(0,r); the Lean definition is total.

  (r : ℝ) (x y : ℝ^n) : ℝ

    Poisson kernel for a ball of radius r.

    The PDE interpretation is for 0 < n, 0 < r, an interior point ‖x‖ < r, and a boundary point ‖y‖ = r. The definition is total, allowing algebraic rewrites without side conditions.

Integrating the kernel against boundary data over the sphere gives the Poisson extension. The definition pulls the y-independent prefactor (r^2-\lVert x\rVert^2)/(n\alpha(n)r) outside the integral, leaving g(y)/\lVert x-y\rVert^n as the integrand; this is the form in which the extension is differentiated.

Proof for Theorem 5.34
uses 0

Insert the explicit formula for K_r(x,y) into the sphere integral. The factor (r^2-\lVert x\rVert^2)/(n\alpha(n)r) is independent of y and can be pulled outside, leaving exactly the prefactor definition of the Poisson extension.

The Poisson extension is meaningful only inside the ball. The Dirichlet candidate glues it to the datum on the sphere and outside, and attaching the data definitionally rather than through a limit is what lets boundary equality be exact and uniqueness be stated as an equation on the closed ball.

The boundary-attached Dirichlet candidate is the total function

u_{r,g}(x)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\int_{\partial B(0,r)}K_r(x,y)g(y)\,dS(y), &\lVert x\rVert<r,\\[6pt] g(x),&\lVert x\rVert\geq r. \end{cases}

Thus it is the Poisson extension in the open ball and agrees definitionally with the prescribed ambient datum outside it.

    The Poisson solution with its prescribed boundary values attached outside the open ball.

Classical harmonicity requires two derivatives, but the same kernel gives every derivative order in the interior. Near a fixed interior point, a smooth cutoff removes the inverse-distance singularity without changing the sphere integral. Mathlib's convolution regularity theorem then gives smoothness.

In positive dimension, for a positive radius and a continuous ambient representative of the boundary datum, differentiation under the sphere integral gives a C^\infty extension on the open ball. The linked theorems allow every regularity order m\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}, both at individual interior points and throughout the ball. Proof for Theorem 5.36
uses 0

Fix an interior point and choose a smaller neighborhood whose distance from the boundary sphere is positive. The differences between points in this neighborhood and points on the sphere lie in a compact annulus away from zero. Replace the inverse-distance kernel by a smooth compactly supported kernel that agrees on this annulus. Its convolution with the boundary datum is smooth and agrees locally with the original potential. Multiplying by the smooth Poisson prefactor preserves every derivative order.

Given the two derivatives, the Laplacian of the extension is the sphere integral of \Delta_xK_r(x,y), and for \lVert y\rVert=r the kernel is harmonic in x. The theorem carries this pointwise cancellation through the integral.

In positive dimension, if r>0, g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is continuous, and x\in B(0,r), then the coordinate Laplacian of the Poisson extension vanishes:

\Delta\!\left(P_rg\right)(x)=0.

The proof differentiates the kernel twice, uses the common norm-square identities, and performs the resulting sphere-integral cancellation.

Proof for Theorem 5.37
uses 0

Use the two derivative formulas justified by interior regularity and sum their diagonal terms. After writing all denominators over \lVert x-y\rVert^{n+4}, the norm-square identities for boundary points \lVert y\rVert=r make the numerator cancel. Integrating the zero kernel Laplacian yields \Delta(P_rg)(x)=0.

Interior regularity and the vanishing Laplacian are exactly the two clauses of the harmonicity predicate. Combining them for the boundary-attached candidate, which agrees with P_rg on the open ball, gives the existence half of the Dirichlet theorem at the C^2 level.

Proof for Theorem 5.38
uses 0

Inside the ball, the boundary-attached solution is definitionally the Poisson extension. Apply its interior C^2 theorem and its pointwise Laplacian-zero theorem; together these are exactly the classical harmonicity predicate on B(0,r).

Harmonicity inside the ball settles nothing about the boundary condition. Boundary recovery rests on the kernel being positive with mass one and concentrating at x_0 as x\to x_0\in\partial B(0,r), so that the Poisson integral of continuous data converges to g(x_0).

In positive dimension, if r>0 and g is continuous, then

u_{r,g}\in C\!\left(\overline{B(0,r)}\right),\qquad u_{r,g}|_{\partial B(0,r)}=g|_{\partial B(0,r)}.

The proof first shows P_rg(x)\to g(x_0) as x\to x_0 through B(0,r) for every x_0\in\partial B(0,r); the attached total solution then gives exact boundary equality.

Proof for Theorem 5.39
uses 0

Subtract g(x_0) inside the Poisson integral and use that the kernel has mass one. Continuity makes this difference uniformly small near x_0, while positivity and concentration of the kernel control the complementary part. This proves the interior limit; the piecewise definition supplies exact boundary values and glues the two continuous pieces on the closed ball.

Uniqueness comes from the maximum principle. The difference of two solutions is harmonic in the ball, continuous on its closure, and zero on the sphere, and two applications of the weak maximum principle force it to vanish. The mean-value property and the derivative estimates use this theorem to identify a harmonic function with its Poisson extension.

Theorem 5.38
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

The three clauses are the interior Laplacian identity, interior C^2 regularity, and pointwise boundary convergence of the Poisson integral.

With uniqueness, the Poisson formula gives the only solution of the ball Dirichlet problem with continuous data. For model domains with explicit geometry, the classical and potential-theoretic routes therefore give the same answer. For general domains, uniqueness instead follows from the maximum principle alone, without an explicit representation (Gilbarg and Trudinger (2001), Theorem 2.5).

5.3.1.2. Green Functions on General Domains🔗

On a general domain the Green function is built the same way, but the corrector has no formula. For a pole x\in\Omega it is the harmonic function \phi^x with \phi^x(y)=\Phi(y-x) on \partial\Omega, and

G(x,y)=\Phi(y-x)-\phi^x(y).

The representation formula and the symmetry G(x,y)=G(y,x) follow Evans (2010) §2.2.4. A weak construction of the corrector uses the Dirichlet solver in H^1, and the barrier theorem for C^1 domains makes it continuous on the closure. Symmetry needs nothing more. The representation formula also needs the normal derivative of \phi^x on the boundary. The construction of that derivative assumes a C^{n+3} boundary, where the boundary regularity theory gives \phi^x\in C^2(\overline\Omega).

Theorem 5.43

✓L∃∀N

For a pole x and a function \phi, the domain Green kernel is

G_\phi(x,y)=\Phi_n(y-x)-\phi(y).

Its gradient field is \nabla_y\Phi_n(y-x) minus the continuous extension of \nabla\phi to \overline\Omega, so the same field gives the interior gradient and the boundary flux. The definition imposes no conditions on \phi; each theorem states the ones it uses.

Let n\ge2 and let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be a bounded open set with C^1 boundary, given by local graphs. For every x\in\Omega there is a function \phi^x that is harmonic in \Omega, continuous on \overline\Omega, equal to \Phi_n(\cdot-x) on \partial\Omega, and a.e. equal to an H^1(\Omega) field whose gradient is orthogonal to the gradients of H^1_0(\Omega). Any other function harmonic in \Omega, continuous on \overline\Omega, with the same boundary values equals \phi^x on \overline\Omega.

The domain need not be connected, and n=2, with its logarithmic kernel, is included.

Proof for Theorem 5.43
uses 1

Change \Phi_n(\cdot-x) inside a small ball around the pole to get a smooth compactly supported function A with the right boundary values. Solve the Dirichlet problem with data A in H^1: its solution U is weakly harmonic, has a harmonic representative, and the barrier theorem for C^1 domains shows that this representative is continuous up to the boundary with the values of A. Uniqueness is the weak maximum principle on \overline\Omega, applied to the difference of two such functions.

used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let n\ge2 and let \Omega be a bounded open set with C^1 boundary. Let u\in C^2(\overline\Omega) solve -\Delta u=f in \Omega with u=g on \partial\Omega, and let x\in\Omega. If \phi is harmonic in \Omega, lies in C^2(\overline\Omega), and equals \Phi_n(\cdot-x) on \partial\Omega, then f\,G_\phi(x,\cdot) is integrable on \Omega, g\,\partial_\nu G_\phi(x,\cdot) is integrable on \partial\Omega, and

u(x)=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g(y)\,\frac{\partial G_\phi}{\partial\nu_y}(x,y)\,dS(y) +\int_\Omega f(y)\,G_\phi(x,y)\,dy.

If the boundary is C^{n+3}, a corrector with these properties exists, and the formula holds with it.

    A Green formula whose harmonic corrector and classical boundary jets are constructed from Cⁿ⁺³ graph geometry. Both integrability clauses are derived.

Proof for Theorem 5.44
uses 1

Green's second identity on \Omega minus a small ball around x, applied to u and \Phi_n(\cdot-x), gives the Newton representation of u(x), which still contains \partial_\nu u on the boundary. The same identity for u and the harmonic \phi, which has no pole, has no interior point term. Subtracting it cancels \partial_\nu u, because \phi=\Phi_n(\cdot-x) on \partial\Omega. On a C^{n+3} boundary the constructed corrector is C^2 up to the boundary by the boundary regularity theory, and the formula applies to it.

Symmetry has a weak proof, and so holds on every bounded C^1 domain with the constructed correctors. Regularize the two poles in disjoint small balls. Each corrector minus its regularized pole lies in H^1_0, so each can be used as a test field in the other's weak equation. The Dirichlet form is symmetric, and evaluating the regularized poles gives G(x,y)=G(y,x).

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let n\ge2 and let \Omega be a bounded open set with C^1 boundary. If \phi^x and \phi^y are harmonic in \Omega, continuous on \overline\Omega, and equal to \Phi_n(\cdot-x) and \Phi_n(\cdot-y) on \partial\Omega, then

\Phi_n(y-x)-\phi^x(y)=\Phi_n(x-y)-\phi^y(x),

that is, G(x,y)=G(y,x). When the correctors are also C^2 up to the boundary, a second proof goes through Green's identity, as in Evans.

Proof for Theorem 5.45
uses 1

By uniqueness, \phi^x and \phi^y are the constructed correctors, which come with H^1 representatives, and the weak argument with regularized poles applies. For C^2 correctors the second proof writes the Green representation of each corrector at the other pole. The two expressions differ by a boundary flux of the antisymmetric pairing of \Phi_n(\cdot-x) and \Phi_n(\cdot-y), and by Green's identity for the two regular correctors. Both integrals vanish.

The disc shows everything at once. For n=2 the corrector is \Phi\big(|x|(y-x^*)\big), a fundamental solution placed at the reflected point x^*=x/|x|^2, so here the corrector has a formula. The left panel shows the level curves of G(x,\cdot), which close up on the circle where G=0. The right panel shows the Poisson kernel -\partial_\nu G for poles at several distances from the centre. Each kernel has total mass one, and they concentrate as the pole approaches the circle.

5.3.1.3. The Half-Space Kernel🔗

Reflection across the boundary hyperplane gives the half-space analogue of Kelvin inversion. The kernel identities, the normalization, and boundary recovery hold in every positive dimension. The half-space Green's function is important both as a model and as the local building block in parametrix constructions for general domains.

In positive dimension, let R(x',x_n)=(x',-x_n) be reflection across the boundary hyperplane. The upper-half-space Green kernel is

G_{\mathbb H}(x,y)=\Phi_n(y-x)-\Phi_n(y-Rx).

The first pole is physical; the reflected image pole lies outside \mathbb H=\{z:z_n>0\} whenever x\in\mathbb H.

  (x y : ℝ^n) : ℝ
    def GreenFunction.halfSpaceGreenFunction
  {n : ℕ} [Fact (0 < n)] (x y : ℝ^n) : ℝ

    Green's function for the half-space, G(x, y) = Φ(y - x) - Φ(y - x̃), where x̃ is the reflection of x in the boundary hyperplane. The first argument is the pole (or source point) and the second the field point; halfSpaceGreenFunction_comm shows that the kernel is symmetric.

Reflection is an isometry fixing the boundary hyperplane and exchanging the two half-spaces, so for x\in\mathbb H the image pole Rx has negative last coordinate and never meets \mathbb H. Away from the physical pole both terms are therefore smooth and harmonic in y\in\mathbb H, in every positive dimension.

Theorem 5.11
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

Both image terms are smooth and harmonic away from their poles. Reflection places the image pole outside the upper half-space, while the physical pole is removed from the asserted domain.

On the boundary itself, where y_n=0, the point y is equidistant from x and Rx, and radiality of \Phi_n makes the two terms equal. Unlike the ball case, no restriction to n\ge2 is needed, because the reflection formula does not depend on the Kelvin branch of the kernel.

Proof for Theorem 5.48
uses 0

Reflection fixes every boundary point y=(y',0) and changes only the sign of the pole's normal coordinate. Hence \lVert y-x\rVert=\lVert y-Rx\rVert. The fundamental solution is radial, so the two image terms agree and their difference is zero.

Integrating the kernel against a source over the half-space gives the Green potential, the volume term of the representation formula. The integrability predicate is kept separate from the integral because Mathlib's Bochner integral is total: the identities that follow are meaningful only where the integrand is integrable.

uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

In positive dimension, for a source f, the method-of-images Green potential is

\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^n_+}f(x) =\int_{\mathbb R^n_+}G_{\mathbb H}(y,x)f(y)\,dy.

The argument order follows the Lean kernel: y is the pole and x is the field point. The integral is a total Mathlib definition, while the Green-potential integrability condition records the analytic domain condition that the displayed integrand is integrable for every x.

    The source lies in the pointwise domain of the half-space Green operator: its Green integrand is Bochner integrable at every evaluation point.

Two consequences follow from the kernel identities alone: the potential vanishes at boundary points because the kernel does, and a tangential reflection that flips the sign of f flips the sign of the potential. Neither uses differentiability of f.

Proof for Theorem 5.50
uses 0

Boundary vanishing follows pointwise from the image-kernel cancellation. For parity, change variables y=R_i z. Tangential reflection preserves the upper half-space and Lebesgue measure, the Green kernel is invariant when both arguments are reflected, and oddness of f supplies the remaining minus sign.

For the potential to solve -\Delta u=f it is compared with the whole-space convolution \Phi_2*f. When f is odd under the boundary reflection, folding the lower half-plane onto the upper one turns the convolution into the method-of-images integral, provided the convolution integrand is integrable in the first place. The logarithmic growth of \Phi_2 makes this a condition on the tails of f, met for instance by continuous L^1 data with a finite logarithmic moment.

Theorem 5.52
Loading preview
Reverse dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.
✓L∃∀N

Let f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R be odd under reflection across the horizontal boundary. Suppose that, for every field point x,

y\longmapsto \Phi_2(x-y)f(y)

is integrable on \mathbb R^2. Then the method-of-images integrand is integrable on the upper half-plane and

\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^2_+}f(x)=(\Phi_2*f)(x).

No compact support is assumed; the hypothesis is the tail condition for the logarithmic kernel. A concrete sufficient condition is that f be continuous and

f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2),\qquad \log(1+|\cdot|)f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2).

These assumptions make the displayed convolution integrable at every x, so odd data in this class have a well-defined half-space Green potential equal to \Phi_2*f.

Split the whole-space integral into the upper and lower half-planes; their common boundary has Lebesgue measure zero. Reflect the lower integral into the upper half-plane. Reflection preserves Lebesgue measure, while oddness of f changes its sign. The reflected lower term is therefore exactly the negative image term in the half-space Green kernel. For the sufficient logarithmic-moment criterion, continuity controls the locally integrable pole. Outside |y|\le |x|+1, use

|\log|x-y|| \le (1+\log(1+|x|))(1+\log(1+|y|))

and dominate by the two L^1 hypotheses.

Compactly supported C^2 sources satisfy the tail condition trivially, and for them the planar convolution theorem gives -\Delta(\Phi_2*f)=f. The identification \mathcal G_{\mathbb R^2_+}f=\Phi_2*f transports this equation to the half-plane Green potential.

Let f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^2) be odd under reflection across the horizontal boundary, so its restriction to \mathbb R^2_+ is represented by an odd whole-space extension. Then the method-of-images integral is integrable at every field point and

\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^2_+}f=\Phi_2*f, \qquad -\Delta\mathcal G_{\mathbb R^2_+}f=f.

Together with boundary cancellation, this is a classical Dirichlet Poisson solution for this source class.

Proof for Theorem 5.52
uses 0

Split the whole-space convolution into upper- and lower-half-plane integrals; the separating boundary hyperplane is Lebesgue null. Reflect the lower-half integral into the upper half-plane. Measure preservation and oddness of f turn it into the negative image term, giving exactly the Green potential. The planar whole-space convolution theorem then supplies the equation -\Delta u=f.

Boundary data enter through the Poisson kernel, the negative outward normal derivative of G_{\mathbb H} at a boundary point: differentiating \Phi_n(y-x)-\Phi_n(y-Rx) in y_n at y_n=0 gives 2x_n/(n\alpha(n)\lVert x-y\rVert^n). As for the ball, we take the closed form as the definition.

Writing \iota(y')=(y',0) for the boundary embedding, the half-space Poisson extension is

(P_{\mathbb H}g)(x) =\frac{2x_n}{n\alpha(n)} \int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}} \frac{g(\iota(y'))}{\lVert x-\iota(y')\rVert^n}\,dy'.

In Lean this is first defined against the pushforward of Lebesgue measure under \iota; the displayed formula is its coordinate realization.

Unlike the sphere, the boundary hyperplane is unbounded, so decay of the integrand at infinity matters. At an interior point the distance to \iota(y') grows like \lVert y'\rVert, and \lVert y'\rVert^{-n} is integrable at infinity on \mathbb R^{n-1} because n>n-1; this is what makes the extension of bounded data well defined.

Proof for Theorem 5.56
uses 0

Let t=x_n>0 and let a be the tangential projection of x. Both t and \lVert y'-a\rVert are bounded by d=\lVert x-\iota(y')\rVert, hence

1+\lVert y'-a\rVert\leq(1+t^{-1})d.

After taking nth powers and reciprocals, the inverse-distance kernel is dominated by a constant multiple of the translated integrable weight (1+\lVert y'-a\rVert)^{-n}.

The coordinate formula for the extension is a rewrite of the pushforward integral rather than an analytic statement. It is the form in which the differentiation, normalization, and trace arguments are carried out.

Proof for Theorem 5.57
uses 0

Unfold the boundary measure as the pushforward of Lebesgue measure under the canonical embedding \iota(y')=(y',0). The pushforward integration formula turns the boundary integral into an integral over \mathbb R^{n-1}; expanding the Poisson kernel produces the displayed constant and denominator.

Interior differentiability follows by differentiating under the integral. On a ball about x_0 of radius (x_0)_n/2, the gradient of \lVert x-\iota(y')\rVert^{-n} is dominated by a multiple of \lVert x_0-\iota(y')\rVert^{-(n+1)}, which decays one power faster than the kernel and is again integrable; boundedness of g on the hyperplane keeps the product integrable.

Proof for Theorem 5.58
uses 0

At an interior point x_0, the ball of radius (x_0)_n/2 remains inside the upper half-space. On this ball, differentiating \lVert x-\iota(y')\rVert^{-n} produces a norm bounded by a constant times \lVert x_0-\iota(y')\rVert^{-(n+1)}. This boundary-coordinate majorant is integrable, so parametric dominated differentiation applies. The scalar prefactor 2x_n/(n\alpha_n) is differentiable by the coordinate projection rule, and the product rule gives the result.

The exact mass of the kernel is the half-space analogue of the ball kernel's mass one, and it means that the extension reproduces constants.

Proof for Theorem 5.59
uses 0

Translation and positive scaling reduce the boundary-distance integral to unit height. For n\geq2, polar coordinates and the substitution u=r^2 turn its radial part into \frac12 B((n-1)/2,1/2). The Beta–Gamma identity, the sphere-area formula, and \Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi give exactly n\alpha_n/2, which cancels the kernel constant. The case n=1 is the integral over the zero-dimensional boundary.

Mass one converts boundary recovery into an approximate-identity argument. Rescaling the boundary variable by the height t turns the extension into the integral of g(\iota(a+tz)) against a fixed integrable kernel; dominated convergence sends this to the integral of the constant g(\iota(a)) against the kernel, and mass one identifies that with g(\iota(a)). The theorem holds a fixed and lets the height decrease to zero.

Proof for Theorem 5.60
uses 0

Translate and rescale the boundary variable by y=a+tz. The extension then has a fixed integrable kernel K_n(z)=|e_n-\iota(z)|^{-n}. Continuity gives pointwise convergence of the rescaled boundary data, while boundedness supplies a constant multiple of K_n as an integrable dominator. Dominated convergence and the exact kernel mass from the normalization calculation give the stated limit.

The boundary limit also holds when the tangential position varies with the height. The boundary convergence theorem proves convergence along every approach from the upper half-space. It requires a measurable ambient datum, a uniform bound on the boundary hyperplane, and continuity of the boundary restriction at the limiting point. There is no bound on the ratio of horizontal displacement to height: after rescaling, the sampled boundary points still approach the same point, and the same integrable kernel dominates the data.

For measurable ambient data uniformly bounded on the boundary, the extension is also C^2 and harmonic in the interior, by the interior regularity theorem and the harmonicity theorem.

5.3.1.4. Fundamental-Solution Convolution🔗

The representation-formula approach to existence starts here: given f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^n), the convolution u=\Phi_n*f is the natural whole-space candidate for -\Delta u=f. The proof has two steps. The derivative-transfer identity \Delta(\Phi_n*f)=\Phi_n*(\Delta f) uses only local integrability of \Phi_n and the two continuous derivatives and compact support of f. The second step identifies \Phi_n*(\Delta f) with -f through the distributional identity -\Delta\Phi_n=\delta_0, which needs singular-kernel analysis and holds in every positive dimension. Together the two steps give classical inversion for every n\ge2 and every f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^n) (Evans, 2010, Theorem 1, pp. 23–25).

Proof for Theorem 5.62
uses 0

Compact support confines every translated derivative of the right factor to a fixed compact set locally in the field variable. Local integrability of the left factor supplies an integrable dominator there. Differentiation under the integral transfers one coordinate derivative to the right factor, and induction repeats this for any finite derivative list.

5.3.1.4.1. Five-dimensional potentials in L²🔗

The same derivative transfer gives estimates on an unbounded domain. The near and far parts of the Newtonian kernel need different bounds.

In dimension five, let f\in L^1(\mathbb R^5)\cap L^2(\mathbb R^5) and u=\Phi_5*f. The defining integral converges absolutely for almost every field point, and u\in L^2(\mathbb R^5). This also applies to any L^2 source that vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact set. No continuity or radial symmetry is needed. If f\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^5), each Cartesian Hessian entry is also in L^2. If f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^5), then for every finite word \alpha of coordinate directions, including the empty word,

\partial^\alpha u=\Phi_5*(\partial^\alpha f)\in L^2(\mathbb R^5).

The linked theorems prove the L^2 membership; the identity itself is the derivative transfer for a locally integrable kernel.

Proof for Theorem 5.63
uses 0

Split \Phi_5 at unit radius. Its near part is in L^1 by local integrability of the kernel. Its far part decays as \lVert X\rVert^{-3} and belongs to L^2: five-dimensional shells have volume proportional to r^4\,dr, so

\int_1^\infty r^4(r^{-3})^2\,dr =\int_1^\infty r^{-2}\,dr<\infty.

Convolution of an L^1 kernel with an L^2 function belongs to L^2 and converges absolutely almost everywhere. Apply this first to the near kernel and f\in L^2, then to f\in L^1 and the far kernel, swapping the convolution variables in the second term. Adding the two absolutely convergent integrals recovers \Phi_5*f and proves its L^2 membership. If an L^2 source vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact set, Cauchy–Schwarz and finite volume give f\in L^1. Continuous compact sources satisfy both hypotheses as well.

Transfer the derivatives onto f and apply the same estimate to each continuous compactly supported source derivative.

Let f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^5) and u=\Phi_5*f. Then -\Delta u=f, and global integration by parts gives

\begin{aligned} \sum_{i,j=1}^5\int_{\mathbb R^5}|\partial_i\partial_j u|^2 &=\int_{\mathbb R^5}|f|^2,\\ \left(\sum_{a=1}^4\int_{\mathbb R^5} |\partial_{y_a}\partial_z u|^2\right)^{1/2} &\le\tfrac12\lVert f\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb R^5)}. \end{aligned}

The full Hessian sum counts both orders of each mixed derivative. The second sum contains just the four axial/transverse entries. These estimates use ordinary five-dimensional volume and the full classical Hessian, including its diagonal local term.

Proof for Theorem 5.64
uses 0

Derivatives through order three are in L^2, so Cauchy–Schwarz makes every product in the two global integrations by parts integrable. Commuting derivatives gives \int(\partial_i\partial_j u)^2=\int(\partial_i^2u)(\partial_j^2u). Summing over i,j yields the squared Laplacian norm. The proved Poisson equation -\Delta u=f identifies that norm with the source norm. No compact support of u or separately prescribed flux at infinity is needed.

For the half constant, put a=\Delta_yu, b=\partial_z^2u, and let M be the sum of the four axial/transverse squared L^2 norms. The same integration by parts gives M=\int ab. Since a+b=\Delta u,

4M=\int_{\mathbb R^5}(a+b)^2-\int_{\mathbb R^5}(a-b)^2 \le\int_{\mathbb R^5}|f|^2.

Taking square roots gives the factor 1/2 in norm.

By density, the full classical Hessian extends uniquely to bounded linear maps on all of L^2(\mathbb R^5), retaining the energy identity and mixed 1/2 bound. For an L^2 source vanishing almost everywhere outside a compact set, the extended entry T_{ij}f is the weak derivative \partial_i\partial_j of \Phi_5*f. For a C^2_c source it agrees almost everywhere with the classical Hessian entry.

    The bounded Newtonian Hessian agrees with the Hessian of a compact C² source. Finite regularity passes through convolution. Its classical Hessian and the extended operator are then weak derivatives of the same potential, so uniqueness identifies them almost everywhere. No principal-value limit or integrability of the classical Hessian is assumed.

Proof for Theorem 5.65
uses 0

Smooth compactly supported sources are dense in L^2(\mathbb R^5). The energy identity bounds every Hessian component by the source norm, so each component extends continuously to the completion. The full energy identity and the mixed bound pass to the limit. Two such continuous maps agree on the dense class and therefore on every L^2 source.

For the weak-derivative identification, approximate a compactly carried L^2 source by smooth sources supported in a fixed compact set. The potentials converge in L^2, the extended Hessian entries converge in L^2, and the integration-by-parts identity against each test function passes to the limit. A C^2_c source has a C^2 potential, whose classical Hessian is also a weak derivative, so uniqueness of weak derivatives gives the almost-everywhere agreement.

For a source radial in the four transverse coordinates, integrating out their angles turns five-dimensional volume into a constant times r^3\,dr\,dz. The resulting radial Laplacian \partial_r^2+3r^{-1}\partial_r+\partial_z^2 also appears in the axisymmetric streamfunction calculation. Applying the Hessian bounds in those coordinates requires identifying the source and derivatives with their radial lifts.

5.3.1.4.2. Returning to the Poisson equation🔗

Moving two coordinate derivatives onto f in each direction gives the second derivatives of \Phi_n*f, whose continuity follows from the same domination, and summing the pure second derivatives under the integral moves the Laplacian onto f.

Proof for Theorem 5.68
uses 1

For n=2 this is the planar theorem. For n\ge3, fix x and apply the Newtonian pole identity \int\Phi_n\Delta\varphi=-\varphi(0) to the translated datum \varphi(y)=f(x+y). Reflecting the integration variable and using \Phi_n(-y)=\Phi_n(y) identify this integral with \bigl(\Phi_n*(\Delta f)\bigr)(x), so the Laplacian transfer gives \Delta(\Phi_n*f)(x)=-f(x). Global C^2 regularity is part of the transfer theorem.

5.3.2. Mean-Value Formulas🔗

5.3.2.1. Sphere and ball mean values🔗

A harmonic function equals the average of its values over every sphere, and over every ball, centered at a point of the domain and contained in it. Stating this requires the sphere and ball integrals themselves, whose normalizations are fixed in terms of \alpha(n) and |S^{n-1}|=n\alpha(n).

Loading preview

✓L∃∀N

Sphere integrals are defined by pulling the Euclidean surface measure on the unit sphere through \omega\mapsto x+r\omega and including the Jacobian |r|^{n-1}. Ball integrals are ordinary restricted Lebesgue integrals. Division by the corresponding surface area or volume gives the normalized averages at positive radius; at radius zero both averages are totalized to u(x). The mean-value theorems therefore assume a positive radius.

The picture returns to the cubic harmonic polynomial checked by CAS in the Elliptic introduction. There, cancellation of second derivatives gave a pointwise equation. The mean-value theorem turns that equation, together with smoothness, into an identity on every contained circle. The plotted averages illustrate one instance; the theorem explains why changing the center or radius preserves the identity.

The spherical mean-value property states the sphere identity as a predicate on functions, with no differentiability attached. Keeping it separate from harmonicity is what allows the two implications between them to be stated and proved independently, and it lets the mean-value boundary principle apply to functions that are only continuous.

The spherical mean-value property on U requires

u(x)=\frac{1}{|\partial B(x,r)|} \int_{\partial B(x,r)}u\,dS

for every x\in U, every r>0, and every closed ball \overline{B(x,r)}\subseteq U. The closed-ball containment is essential: the spherical integral evaluates the function on the boundary itself.

In positive dimension, if u is integrable on B(x,r) and r\ge 0, then

\int_{B(x,r)}u(y)\,dy =\int_0^r\left(\int_{\partial B(x,\rho)}u\,dS\right)d\rho.

Proof for Theorem 5.71
uses 0

Translate the center to zero, apply Mathlib's polar integration formula with the radial Jacobian measure, identify the inner integral with the defined sphere integral, and translate back. The annulus formula follows by subtracting the nested ball integrals and splitting the radial interval.

Harmonicity enters through the ball Dirichlet problem. A function harmonic on a set containing a closed ball is the Poisson extension of its own boundary trace, and at the center of the ball the Poisson kernel is the constant 1/|\partial B(x,r)|, so evaluating the Poisson integral at the center gives exactly the spherical average. The uniqueness theorem that justifies the identification follows from the weak maximum principle.

Proof for Theorem 5.72
uses 1

For an admissible ball, translate its center to the origin, extend the continuous boundary trace, solve the ball Dirichlet problem by the Poisson kernel, and use the maximum-principle uniqueness theorem to identify the original function with the Poisson solution. Evaluation at the center gives the spherical average.

The converse implication needs a maximum principle that assumes only the mean-value property, since a function with the mean-value property is not assumed differentiable. The boundary principle supplies it, with mean-value rigidity replacing the second-derivative test used for harmonic functions.

The minimum statement follows by applying the maximum statement to -u.

Conversely, in positive dimension, let U\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open. If u is continuous on U and has the spherical mean-value property on every closed ball contained in U, then u is C^2 on U and satisfies \Delta u=0 there. Together with the forward implication, this characterizes classical harmonic functions by their spherical averages.

Definition 5.35
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

Openness of U gives a small closed ball around each point. Continuously extend the boundary trace and form its Poisson solution. The difference from u has the mean-value property and zero boundary values, so the mean-value boundary principle makes it vanish throughout the ball. Local equality with the smooth Poisson solution supplies both C^2 regularity and the vanishing Laplacian.

Evans proves the mean-value formula by differentiating the sphere average in the radius and showing, through the divergence theorem, that the derivative is proportional to the flux of Du through the sphere, which vanishes for harmonic u. The theorem is the differentiation step of that argument, for globally C^1 fields; the two characterization theorems rest on the Poisson construction.

In positive dimension and at positive radii, the normalized geometric sphere average equals the average over the fixed unit sphere, because the radial Jacobian cancels the surface-area scaling. If u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is globally C^1, then differentiation under this fixed finite measure gives

\frac{d}{dr}\left( \frac{1}{|\partial B(x,r)|}\int_{\partial B(x,r)}u\,dS \right) =\frac1{|\partial B(0,1)|} \int_{\partial B(0,1)}Du(x+r\omega)\,\omega\,dS(\omega).

For a function defined only on an open domain, the formula applies after a C^1 extension from a neighborhood of the closed ball.

Proof for Theorem 5.75
uses 0

Rewrite the normalized sphere average on radius r as an integral over the fixed unit sphere; the Jacobian and surface-area factors cancel. Global C^1 regularity permits differentiation under this finite measure, and the chain rule differentiates u(x+r\omega) to Du(x+r\omega)\,\omega.

Ball averages follow from sphere averages by integrating in the radius. If u(x) equals the sphere average at every radius \rho\le r, then multiplying by the area of \partial B(x,\rho) and integrating from 0 to r gives u(x)|B(x,r)| on one side and, by the coarea formula, the ball integral on the other. Integrability of u on the ball is the hypothesis the coarea formula needs.

uses 1

The spherical identity is the defining property. The ball identity follows by the coarea formula: substitute the spherical identity at every intermediate radius and integrate the surface areas from 0 to r.

5.3.3. Interior Derivative Estimates🔗

5.3.3.1. Derivative estimates and Liouville's theorem🔗

Interior derivative estimates express the rigidity of harmonic functions quantitatively: the derivatives of u at a point are controlled by the size of u on any surrounding sphere or ball. The proof identifies u with the Poisson extension of its boundary trace and differentiates the Poisson kernel at the center, which yields the constant n/r without assuming in advance that the derivatives are harmonic.

Proof for Theorem 5.77
uses 1

Translate the ball to the origin, extend the boundary trace, and identify the translated function locally with its Poisson extension. Differentiating the Poisson kernel at the center and estimating the resulting spherical integral by Cauchy–Schwarz gives the explicit constant nM/r.

Replacing the boundary supremum by an integral of |u| costs the volume of a half-radius ball: the boundary estimate is applied on B(x,r/2), and |u| at each point of its sphere is bounded by the ball average of |u| over a ball of radius r/2 that still lies inside B(x,r). The constant 2^{n+1}n/\alpha(n) produced this way is Evans's.

Theorem 5.76
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

Apply the boundary-supremum estimate on the half-radius ball. At each point of its boundary sphere, apply the ball mean-value formula on the ball of radius r/2 centered there. These smaller open balls lie in B(x,r); the triangle inequality, monotonicity of the integral of |u|, and |B(0,r/2)|=\alpha(n)(r/2)^n give Evans's constant.

Iterating the first-order estimate bounds derivatives of every order, and each iteration spends part of the available radius: to control D^ku at x, one estimates D^{k-1}u on a sphere of radius r_0 about x, each point of which must still have a ball of radius r_1+\dots+r_{k-1} inside the domain. The sum of radii records this nested geometry.

In positive dimension, let u be harmonic on an open set U, let k be any natural number, and assign a positive radius budget r_i to each derivative step. If

\overline{B\left(x,\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}r_i\right)}\subseteq U, \qquad |u|\le M \quad\text{on this ball},

then

\lVert D^k u(x)\rVert\le \frac{n^kM}{\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}r_i}.

Taking every r_i=r gives the uniform estimate on \overline{B(x,kr)} with denominator r^k. In particular, k=2 and k=3 recover the usual second- and third-derivative nested-ball estimates. The order-zero case is included.

Proof for Theorem 5.79
uses 1

First derive harmonicity of the evaluated derivatives from harmonicity of u on the open domain. Then induct on k, spending the head radius in the final first-derivative estimate. On its boundary sphere, the induction hypothesis controls the preceding iterated derivative using the tail radii. Apply the first-order estimate to each multilinear evaluation and use the operator norm to reassemble the directional bounds. Constant radius budgets give the uniform theorem; replacing k by k+1 gives the successor form.

Liouville's theorem is the limiting case of the boundary-supremum estimate on all of \mathbb R^n: if |u|\le M everywhere, then \lVert Du(x)\rVert\le nM/r for every r>0, so Du vanishes identically and u is constant.

Proof for Theorem 5.80
uses 1

Apply the boundary-supremum derivative estimate on arbitrarily large balls. If the derivative norm were positive, choosing a radius larger than its bound would give a strict contradiction. Mathlib's zero-derivative constancy theorem then identifies every value with the value at the origin.

5.3.4. Maximum, Minimum, Comparison, and Uniqueness for Harmonic Functions🔗

5.3.4.1. From mean values to rigidity🔗

Maximum principles turn local harmonicity into global order information. The weak principle says that a harmonic function continuous up to the boundary of a ball cannot rise above its boundary values. Applying it to a difference gives comparison, and applying comparison in both directions gives uniqueness for the ball Dirichlet problem.

The strong principle has a different conclusion. On an open preconnected domain, an interior point at which a harmonic function attains its domain-wide maximum forces the function to be constant. The proof uses the spherical mean-value identity: an average can equal a pointwise upper bound only when the surrounding values also equal that bound. The maximum set is therefore both open and closed.

uses 0

Proof for Theorem 5.82
uses 1

The function -u is harmonic whenever u is. The boundary inequality m\leq u is equivalent to -u\leq-m, so the weak maximum principle gives -u(x)\leq-m throughout the closed ball. Negating this inequality yields m\leq u(x).

Comparison is the weak maximum principle for the difference u-v: harmonicity is preserved under subtraction, and the boundary inequality u\le v is the boundary bound u-v\le0. This is the form in which the principle is applied to two candidate solutions of the same Dirichlet problem.

Proof for Theorem 5.84
uses 1

Because the two harmonic functions agree on the boundary, the comparison principle applied to u and v gives u\leq v on the closed ball. Applying it again with the functions exchanged gives v\leq u; pointwise antisymmetry then gives u=v.

The strong principle replaces the ball by an arbitrary open preconnected set and the boundary hypothesis by an interior maximum. Its proof uses the spherical mean-value identity instead of the second-derivative test. Our proof of the mean-value formula goes through the ball Poisson theory, so the strong principle also depends on the weak one.

    Strong maximum principle in Evans' global-maximum form.

    If a PDE-harmonic function on a connected open domain attains its domain-wide maximum at an interior point, then it is constant throughout the domain.

Proof for Theorem 5.85
uses 1

At a maximum point, the spherical mean-value identity says that the continuous nonnegative gap u(x_0)-u has integral zero on every sufficiently small centered sphere. Positivity of surface measure on open patches forces the gap to vanish on each sphere. Varying the radius fills a ball, so the maximum set is open in U. It is also relatively closed by continuity and contains x_0; preconnectedness makes it all of U.

With its minimum counterpart, the strong principle says that a nonconstant harmonic function on a preconnected open set attains neither its maximum nor its minimum over the set.

Proof for Theorem 5.86
uses 1

Negation preserves harmonicity. If u attains its minimum at x_0, then -u attains its maximum there. The strong maximum principle makes -u constant on the preconnected domain, and multiplying the resulting identity by -1 makes u constant as well.

5.3.4.2. Operators with variable coefficients🔗

The Laplacian is the simplest of the operators

Lu=-\sum_{i,j=1}^n a^{ij}(x)\,\partial_i\partial_j u+\sum_{i=1}^n b^i(x)\,\partial_i u+c(x)\,u

studied in Evans (2010) §6.4. The mean-value identity is lost as soon as the coefficients vary, so these principles need a different argument. Both proofs perturb u by an explicit function whose image under L has a known sign, and then look at a maximum point with the second-derivative test. The sign conventions follow Evans, so -\Delta is the case a=I, b=0, c=0, and a subsolution is a function with Lu\le0.

The matrix a(x) may be any real matrix. Only its quadratic form enters the hypotheses, and that form depends only on the symmetric part of a(x). The Lean proofs first replace a by its symmetric part, which changes neither Lu (the Hessian of a C^2 function is symmetric) nor the quadratic form. The weak and strong principles and the Hopf lemma assume no continuity of the coefficients.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open with compact closure. Suppose that on \Omega the quadratic form of a(x) is nonnegative, that for one fixed index i we have a_{ii}\ge\alpha>0 and b^i\le B, and that c\ge0. u\le M\qquad\text{on }\overline\Omega.

When c=0 the bound M may have either sign. When c\ge0 is nonzero somewhere, M must be nonnegative there, which is the form u\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u^+ of Evans's statement.

Proof for Theorem 5.88
uses 1

Replace a by its symmetric part. Put e(x)=e^{\lambda x_i} and let E be its maximum over the compact set \overline\Omega. Without the potential, e has residual (-\lambda^2a_{ii}+\lambda b^i)e\le(-\lambda^2\alpha+\lambda B)e, which is negative once \lambda\alpha>B. The shifted barrier e-E is nonpositive, so the potential adds c(e-E)\le0 and L(e-E)<0. For \varepsilon>0 the function u_\varepsilon=u+\varepsilon(e-E) is a strict subsolution with u_\varepsilon\le M on the boundary. At an interior maximum above M its gradient would vanish, its Hessian would be negative semidefinite, and c\,u_\varepsilon\ge cM\ge0, which together give Lu_\varepsilon\ge0. Hence u_\varepsilon\le M, and letting \varepsilon\to0 gives the claim.

The strong principle needs to know how u leaves a boundary maximum. The Hopf lemma answers that it leaves at a definite rate. At a point of an interior tangent ball where u attains a strict maximum, the outward normal derivative is strictly positive. A plain maximum only gives \partial_\nu u\ge0.

In the figure the gap u(x^0)-u along the inner radius stays above a multiple of the barrier v=e^{-\lambda|x|^2}-e^{-\lambda}. The barrier vanishes on the outer sphere with a nonzero slope, so the gap has a nonzero slope too. A function whose gap grows only quadratically would cross the barrier, and the comparison principle on the annulus rules that out.

On the annulus R/2<\lVert x-z\rVert<R assume the quadratic form of a is at least \kappa|v|^2 with \kappa>0, \operatorname{tr}a\le A, \lVert b\rVert\le B, 0\le c\le C, c\,u(x^0)\ge0, and Lu\le0. Let u be continuous on \overline B(z,R), C^2 in B(z,R), differentiable at x^0, and suppose u(x)<u(x^0) for every x\in B(z,R). Then

Du(x^0)\,\nu>0,\qquad \nu=\frac{x^0-z}{R}.

The second Lean statement gives the same conclusion as a one-sided inward derivative along the segment from x^0 to z, and does not need differentiability of u at x^0.

    A strict boundary maximum for an arbitrary real-matrix subsolution has negative inward radial derivative. The matrix is uniformly elliptic in the quadratic-form sense on the outer annulus; its trace, the drift norm, and the nonnegative potential have upper bounds there. The condition c(x)u(x₀) ≥ 0 replaces a sign restriction on the maximum. Principal factors are constructed from the self-adjoint part of the matrix.

Proof for Theorem 5.89
uses 1

Set v(x)=e^{-\lambda\lVert x-z\rVert^2}-e^{-\lambda R^2}. For \lambda large, depending on \kappa, A, B, C, and R, the barrier satisfies Lv\le0 on the annulus. On the inner sphere u<u(x^0) holds with a positive gap by compactness, so for small \varepsilon the function u+\varepsilon v-u(x^0) is at most 0 on both boundary spheres. The weak principle on the annulus gives u(x^0)-u\ge\varepsilon v. Differentiating this at x^0 along the inward radius yields a derivative at most \varepsilon\,\partial_\nu v(x^0)<0.

The strong principle follows. If u attains its maximum over a connected open set at an interior point and is not constant, some ball inside the set touches the maximum set at a boundary point. At that point Du=0 because it is an interior maximum, while Hopf's lemma makes a directional derivative positive.

Let \Omega be open and preconnected. Assume that each point of \Omega has a closed ball in \Omega on which the quadratic form of a is at least \kappa|v|^2 with \kappa>0, and \operatorname{tr}a, \lVert b\rVert, and c\ge0 are bounded above. If u is C^2 in \Omega, Lu\le0, u attains its maximum over \Omega at x^0\in\Omega, and c\,u(x^0)\ge0, then u\equiv u(x^0) on \Omega.

The constants may change from ball to ball; bounded continuous coefficients on a connected domain, with c\ge0 and a nonnegative maximum, are a special case.

    Strong maximum principle for arbitrary real principal matrices. Local quadratic ellipticity and upper bounds for the trace, drift norm, and nonnegative potential suffice. The maximum is attained in the open connected domain and satisfies cM ≥ 0; no symmetry or coefficient continuity is assumed.

Proof for Theorem 5.90
uses 1

Replace a by its symmetric part. The set where u=u(x^0) is closed in \Omega and nonempty. If it were not all of \Omega, there would be a point of the complement closer to the maximum set than to \partial\Omega, and a ball around it, inside \Omega and in the set u<u(x^0), touching the maximum set at a boundary point y. At y the derivative vanishes, since y is an interior maximum. The Hopf lemma on this ball, with the local constants, says a normal derivative is positive. The contradiction shows the maximum set is open as well.

5.3.4.3. Harnack comparison🔗

The maximum principle compares an interior value with boundary data. Harnack compares two interior values using positivity. If \lVert x-y\rVert\le r, then B(y,r)\subset B(x,2r), and mean values and u\ge0 give

u(y)=\frac{1}{|B(y,r)|}\int_{B(y,r)}u \le\frac{1}{|B(y,r)|}\int_{B(x,2r)}u =2^n u(x).

Positivity is the step that permits enlarging the integration region. A function that changes sign can lose mass by cancellation, so the same argument would fail. This also explains why a nonnegative harmonic function cannot vanish at an interior point and be positive just beside it.

On the unit disc the Poisson kernel makes the comparison exact. Every positive harmonic function is an average of the kernels P(\cdot,\zeta) over boundary points \zeta, and each kernel satisfies

\frac{1-r}{1+r}\le\frac{P(x,\zeta)}{P(0,\zeta)}\le\frac{1+r}{1-r}\qquad(|x|=r<1).

The figure plots these ratios along one radius. The band is the whole of the Harnack inequality on the disc. On |x|\le\tfrac12 it gives \sup u\le9\inf u, and the constant blows up like (1-r)^{-2} as the smaller disc grows toward the boundary. The formal proof chains mean-value balls instead of using the Poisson kernel, which gives a worse constant on any compact set but works in every domain.

    Local Harnack inequality on a ball, following Evans §2.2.3.

    If u is nonnegative and harmonic on a set containing B̄(x, 2r), then dist x y ≤ r implies u(y) ≤ 2ⁿ u(x). No openness assumption on the ambient set is needed because the closed-ball containment is explicit.

Proof for Theorem 5.91
uses 1

The ball B(y,r) lies inside B(x,2r). Nonnegativity makes the integral over the smaller ball no larger than the integral over the larger one. Applying the ball mean-value formula at y and x, then using |B(x,2r)|=2^n|B(y,r)|, gives the stated factor.

To compare distant points, we pass through a chain of overlapping balls, each link costing a factor 2^n. The constant can deteriorate as the compact set approaches the boundary or as the connecting geometry forces more links.

u(x)\leq C\,u(y)\qquad(x,y\in K).

    Uniform Harnack comparison on a compact subset of a connected domain.

    This is the global compactly-contained form of Evans §2.2.3. If K is a compact subset of the open preconnected set U, there is a positive constant C, chosen independently of u, such that every nonnegative PDE-harmonic function on U satisfies u(x) ≤ C u(y) for x, y ∈ K. The set K itself need not be connected because the comparison chains may travel through U.

Proof for Theorem 5.92
uses 1

Join points of the connected domain by chains of overlapping admissible balls. Each link contributes the local factor 2^n. Compactness gives a finite subcover of K and hence a uniform bound on the number of links needed from a fixed base point. Comparing both x and y with that base point produces one constant valid for every pair in K.

The same inequality holds for nonnegative solutions of Lu=0 with variable coefficients, which is Theorem 5 of Evans (2010) §6.4.3. There is no mean-value formula in this setting. The Lean proof uses the contact-set method, with the monotone envelope, contact Jacobian, and basic measure estimate following Imbert and Silvestre's lecture notes on fully nonlinear equations (§§4.1 to 4.2 of the 2013 HAL version). No derivative of a coefficient is taken anywhere.

The first step is a quantitative form of the strong principle: a nonnegative supersolution without potential that is small at one point is small on a set of definite measure.

Proof for Theorem 5.93
uses 0

Slide each paraboloid with vertex y\in\overline B(x^0,\tfrac18) up until it touches u from below on \overline B(0,\tfrac{15}{16}). Because u(x^0)\le1 and u\ge0 on the unit ball, the touching happens at an interior point where u\le\tfrac54. The contact set is compact and the map sending a contact point to its vertex covers the vertex ball. At a contact point the contact Jacobian J is positive semidefinite, and Lu\ge0 together with the gradient identity at contact gives \alpha\operatorname{tr}J\le\operatorname{tr}(aJ)\le\tau+2B. This bounds \det J by ((\tau+2B)/\alpha)^n, and the area formula gives the estimate.

Covering the unit cube by dyadic subcubes and applying this estimate at every scale turns one point of smallness into geometric decay of the superlevel sets. This is the L^\varepsilon estimate, and it controls \inf u from below.

Proof for Theorem 5.94
uses 1

The contact estimate, rescaled to cubes, says that u\le M on a fixed fraction \eta of a cube whenever u\le1 at a point of a slightly larger cube. Apply it to u/M^k. A dyadic child in which \{u>M^{k+1}\} has density above 1-\eta cannot contain a point of its parent where u\le M^k. Mathlib's subbox partition theorem turns this into the induction that loses the factor \delta=1-\eta at each level.

A matching upper estimate for subsolutions and a chain of cubes across the domain finish the proof. The signed potential is absorbed by multiplying u by an exponential in an added coordinate, which turns c into a drift in one more dimension.

Let U be open and bounded and let V be preconnected with \overline V\subseteq U. Let a, b, c be continuous on U with bounded ranges, with a symmetric and \sum_{i,j}a_{ij}(x)v_iv_j\ge\alpha|v|^2 for almost every x\in U, where \alpha>0. There is C>0 such that every u\in C^2(U) with u\ge0 and Lu=0 in U satisfies

\sup_V u\le C\,\inf_V u.

The potential c may have either sign. The second Lean statement replaces the bounded ranges by essential bounds.

Proof for Theorem 5.95
uses 1

Continuity turns the almost-everywhere bounds and ellipticity into pointwise ones on the open set U. Compactness of \overline V and connectedness of V give a finite chain of small balls in U. On each ball the level decay bounds the infimum from below and the upper estimate bounds the supremum, with constants fixed by \alpha, the coefficient bounds, and the radius. Multiplying along the chain gives one constant for all pairs of points of V.

5.3.5. Radial Symmetry by Moving Planes🔗

5.3.5.1. Reflecting a cap🔗

The maximum principle also proves symmetry. Let u>0 solve

-\Delta u=f(u)\quad\text{in }B(0,1),\qquad u=0\quad\text{on }\partial B(0,1),

with f Lipschitz. The equation is invariant under rotations, but nothing in the hypotheses says that u is. Gidas et al. (1979) showed that it must be radial and strictly decreasing in |x|. The version proved here is Theorem 2 of Evans (2010) §9.5.2.

Fix a unit vector e and a number \lambda\in[0,1). The hyperplane x\cdot e=\lambda cuts off the cap \Sigma_\lambda=\{x\in B(0,1):x\cdot e>\lambda\}, and reflection across the plane sends x to x^\lambda. Because \lambda\ge0, the mirror image of the cap lies in the ball again. The difference w_\lambda(x)=u(x^\lambda)-u(x) is defined on the cap, vanishes on the flat face, and is nonnegative on the spherical face, where u=0.

The figure shows the plane moving from \lambda=\tfrac12 toward the centre for the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of the disc. Along the whole motion the reflected profile stays above the original one, and at \lambda=0 the two agree. The theorem says the same happens for every positive solution and every direction e.

The first step is a sign. Subtracting the equations at x and x^\lambda and using the Lipschitz bound turns the nonlinear equation into a linear inequality for w_\lambda, with the Lipschitz constant as potential. The strong maximum principle then makes a nonnegative w_\lambda strictly positive.

Let u be C^2 on \mathbb R^n, positive in B(0,1), zero on the sphere, and a solution of -\Delta u=f(u) in the ball, with f Lipschitz with constant L. Let e be a unit vector and \lambda>0. Wherever w_\lambda\ge0 in the cap,

-\Delta w_\lambda+L\,w_\lambda\ge0.

If w_\lambda\ge0 on all of \Sigma_\lambda, then w_\lambda(x)>0 at every x of the closed ball with x\cdot e>\lambda.

Proof for Theorem 5.96
uses 1

The Laplacian commutes with reflection, so -\Delta w_\lambda=f(u(x^\lambda))-f(u(x))\ge-L\,w_\lambda when w_\lambda\ge0. The cap is convex and so connected. On its spherical face u=0 while u(x^\lambda)>0, because \lambda>0 puts x^\lambda inside the ball. So w_\lambda is positive somewhere, and the strong principle for -\Delta+L rules out an interior zero.

The plane then moves, from \lambda=1, where the cap is empty, down to \lambda=0. The set of parameters at which w_\lambda\ge0 is closed by continuity, and strict comparison together with the Hopf lemma on the flat face makes it open, so it is all of (0,1].

Let u be C^2 on \mathbb R^n, positive in B(0,1), zero on the sphere, and a solution of -\Delta u=f(u) in the ball with f Lipschitz. For every unit vector e, every \lambda\ge0, and every x\in B(0,1) with x\cdot e>\lambda,

u(x)\le u(x^\lambda).

    The semilinear equation implies reflection comparison at every plane between the center and the positive pole, and vacuously at every higher plane.

Proof for Theorem 5.97
uses 1

For \lambda\ge1 the cap is empty. Closedness of the good set of parameters follows from continuity of u. For openness at a good \lambda>0, strict comparison gives w_\lambda>0 in the cap and the Hopf lemma gives \partial_eu<0 on the flat face. Near the sphere, a separate argument shows that u decreases along every outward-pointing direction. By the Hopf lemma \partial_\nu u can vanish on the sphere only when f(0)<0, and there the Hessian supplies the sign. Compactness makes these neighbourhoods uniform, so every nearby plane is good. The interval is connected, and the case \lambda=0 is a limit.

At \lambda=0 comparison holds in the directions e and -e, so u is even under reflection in every hyperplane through the origin, and any two points of the same norm are exchanged by one such reflection.

Definition 5.1
Loading preview
Group member preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.
uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be Lipschitz, and let u be C^2 up to the boundary of B(0,1), with

-\Delta u=f(u)\ \text{ and }\ u>0\ \text{ in }B(0,1),\qquad u=0\ \text{ on }\partial B(0,1).

Then there is a continuous v:[0,1]\to[0,\infty) that is strictly decreasing on [0,1], with v(1)=0 and

u(x)=v(|x|)\qquad(x\in\overline B(0,1)).

    Radial symmetry on the unit ball, Evans's §9.5.2, Theorem 2: a positive solution of -Δu = f(u) that is C² up to the boundary and vanishes on the sphere is v(‖x‖) for a continuous profile v ≥ 0 that is strictly decreasing on [0, 1] with v(1) = 0. As in Evans, f is Lipschitz; since u is bounded, a locally Lipschitz reaction can be replaced by a Lipschitz one that agrees with it on the range of u. The zero-dimensional case is included directly. No derivative or sign of the reaction, ambient extension, or comparison is assumed.

Proof for Theorem 5.98
uses 1

Extend u from the closed ball to a C^2 function on \mathbb R^n; the equation only involves the open ball, so it is unchanged. Continuation at \lambda=0 in the directions \pm e gives u(x)=u(x^0). For |x|=|y| and x\ne y, take e=(x-y)/|x-y|; the reflection with \lambda=0 sends x to y, so u(x)=u(y). Define v(r)=u(re_1). For 0\le r<s\le1, strict comparison at \lambda=(r+s)/2 in the direction e_1 compares se_1 with its mirror image re_1 and gives v(s)<v(r). Dimension zero is handled separately.

The theorem is stated for globally Lipschitz f. Since u is bounded, only the values of f on the range of u matter, so a locally Lipschitz f can be modified outside that range. The conclusion is strict monotonicity on the closed interval: v(s)<v(r) whenever 0\le r<s\le1.
